A team of UC Santa Barbara student historians with a passion for undergraduate education has turned the disruptive nature of the internet on its head by creating a platform that requires users’ active, collaborative participation—in contrast to the more passive encounters typical of web browsing.
This online tool, which is free to use for faculty, librarians, and students, was designed to improve students’ learning of world history as they engage in debates over provocative questions. The site, historybayes.org, includes more than 200 guided activities that center around modern world history topics.
The platform originated in the UC Santa Barbara history department, where two lecturers with expertise in both medieval and pre-modern societies conceived a new way to teach history through active, critical engagement. After receiving an Academic Senate grant to design the site, Susanne Habicht and Zeev Wachtel teamed up with other members of the department: Director of the Center for Evidence-Based Writing (EW) Laura M. Fine and neuroscientist Howard Chizeck, professor emeritus, who is an expert in problem solving and decision-making. They also recruited student assistants.
The platform is the first product to evolve from EW, which features resources, training, and targeted help for faculty integrating evidence-based learning and writing in lower division courses. Under the new leadership of Fine, who recently was appointed to a three-year term as EW director, the center continues to assist UCSB faculty in integrating evidence-based learning principles into their courses.
The new online tool also reflects a growing trend toward the use of electronic media in undergraduate education in place of moderated anonymous online discussion groups, which have been shown to illustrate a digital equivalent of “the tragedy of the commons,” where participants engage in antisocial behavior that runs counter to the common benefit.
Far from an anonymous forum, historybayes.org promotes a situation of mutual observation that encourages users to challenge each other politely as they consider alternative interpretations of historical evidence and plausible explanations. The more deeply learners engage, the more they build a shared understanding. They are rewarded not just for their individual contribution but also for synthesizing information from various students’ ideas in order to present the most plausible argument addressing the guiding question.
“A community builds up around your contribution, and you learn a great deal more than you would have by just reading an answer,” said Tanner Hubbert, a UCSB sophomore majoring in history and the soon-to-be appointed first historybayes.org student ambassador.
EW’s student program coordinator, Wanda V. Hudson, agrees: “In passive web browsing you often fail to grasp important concepts. In our tool, you know immediately whether you’re on the right track. You must draw legitimate conclusions from empirical evidence in order to score points.”
The new resource has been tested with UCSB history students, and participating faculty have reported positive results. Mark Brillon, faculty developer for teaching and learning with technology at UC Santa Cruz, also found a great deal to praise in a recent evaluation. Brillon pointed out the site’s use of the Socratic method to help students learn via questioning and debate. Now that the beta version is ready, the course creators are soliciting feedback from historians to refine their tool and learn more about its future applications.
Throughout the summer, EW staff and students will prepare the site’s activities for publication on the web, add more evidence for historians to examine, and expand the range of debated topics and discussion prompts. New questions will be tagged according to the relevant historical time periods, regions, and themes, and will carry tags, such as causation, relativism, sources, and controversies. During the first semester the aging platform will continue to undergo improvements, learning from participants’ feedback.
Ultimately, the system will become independent and adaptive, and will generate questions, arguments, and historical data specific to teachers’ needs. Ideally, the tool will allow students to customize the level of difficulty of the platform’s questions, arguments and evidence according to their abilities.
In the future, historybayes.org could support other disciplines that rely on evidence-based, argument-driven learning, such as law and cognitive science.
A cocktail party, a concert, a chamber ensemble, another concert, and dinner with world-renowned guests. Not bad for a Friday evening. Friday Club is a longstanding annual tradition at the MFA Program for Poets and Writers at Warren Wilson College. Once a month, for eight months, a whole bunch of Warren Wilson MFA students, faculty and guest writers gather in someone’s house or apartment to read and talk, with snacks, beer and wine provided. It’s a chance for students to put themselves (and their work!) out there, to try on different voices, to roughhouse with their peers, and generally have a good time.
Friday Club readings are followed by dinner, and conversation – about craft, about politics, about poetry and about each other’s works in progress. Francis and I try to come to as many Friday Club events as possible. One Friday, in particular, stands out in my mind, and you’re all invited to our virtual Friday Club, where you can sample some of the work that was presented that evening.
In alphabetical order, Sarah, Michelle, Joe, Tara, Poe, Lisa, Priscilla, Margaret and Katie read short fiction. (I skipped this part of the evening, because I was dishing out baked ziti.) However, I made sure to stay for the poetry readings. Tara read a clear and compelling description of a difficult medical condition. Priscilla read a haunting love poem in which her partner speaks from beyond the grave. Lisa played charmingly with words, helping us to see the world as fresh as a spring dawn. Margaret read a sweet sensual celebration of old age. Poet Katie read several poems, including one about the death of her dog, a hilarious Las Vegas Methodist Church poem and a sestina about watching her friend’s son play t-ball. Each time she read a new poem, Katie said, “Now this is a poem,” and we all knew she was right.
Michelle dared us to consider people we thought we knew. Joe asked us to accept a different path than the one we’re on. Margaret considered, with great imagination, the effects of what-ifs. Lisa visited the town dump. Tara considered and Jo Ann listed the ways a husband tries to make her ill. Poe responded to the challenge of writing a poem and found that, in essence, he was writing about himself. Sarah went diving in the underworld. Priscilla celebrated her Jewish heritage. Louise read an elegy to her father; and Katie wondered who might stop the rain.
So join us at our virtual Friday Club, where we’re going to present a little bit of what we heard that night. The first writer to share below will be Katie, our star Friday Clubper that night. We hope you like what we’re serving here and that you too will be moved to share some of your own work with your favorite virtual crowd.

We hope you’ll shamelessly indulge our desire to talk about poetry and inspire some new work. After all, the best way to rise to the top of your game is to ponder the thoughts of the folks who came before you.
